tr.td: 13 April 1948 (given as 14 April in one account)
Sheikh Jarrah, Jerusalem, on the road to Mount Scopus
A Jewish convoy of doctors, nurses, university staff, patients and Haganah escorts bound for Hadassah Hospital and the Hebrew University
Arab forces; no one was prosecuted, according to the Jerusalem Post
Two ambulances, two or three buses, three supply trucks and two Haganah escort vehicles, according to the accounts opened for this entry
Lieutenant Asher "Zizi" Rahav of the Haganah, according to a Hadassah history
Dr. Haim Yassky, director of Hadassah Hospital
Dr. Leonid Doljansky, Dr. Moshe Ben-David, Dr. Guenther Wolfsohn and Professor Enzo Bonaventura (Dov Joseph's list)
About seven hours according to Dov Joseph; 9:30 a.m. to at least 5 p.m. according to the Jerusalem Post
Twenty-eight people, eight of them unhurt, according to Joseph
A British post stood within a few hundred yards; accounts of the Haganah and Hadassah say the army did not intervene for hours
The Arab Higher Committee praised the attack; Arab sources quoted by the Jerusalem Post said the convoy was a military formation
31 victims identified and buried singly; the rest in a mass grave at Sanhedria Cemetery, with 22 reported missing
The hospital on Mount Scopus was largely evacuated and did not reopen until after 1967

content.p: On the morning of 13 April 1948 a column of ambulances, buses and trucks left the centre of Jewish Jerusalem for Mount Scopus, where the Hadassah hospital and the Hebrew University stood cut off behind an Arab district. The road was only about three miles long, but it ran through Sheikh Jarrah. Within the hour a mine had stopped the lead vehicle, and the rest of the column was caught between stone walls under fire. By late afternoon the toll was somewhere between 77 and 79 dead, most of them doctors, nurses, students and university staff. Among them was the hospital's director, Dr. Haim Yassky.

The attack is also remembered for what did not happen. A British post stood within a few hundred yards of the shooting, and Jewish accounts, from survivors to the hospital's own history, say that help was slow in coming. The British, the Haganah and the Arab side each gave a different account at the time, and some points are still argued.

After the United Nations voted to partition Palestine in November 1947, fighting spread through the country. In Jerusalem the Jewish institutions on Mount Scopus, the hospital and the university campus, could be reached only by the Sheikh Jarrah road. The Jerusalem Post describes that road as plagued by mines and sniper fire, and says the blockade had left the hospital struggling for supplies. Convoys went up under British protection: Dov Joseph, in his 1960 book The Faithful City, said the Jewish side had been sending relief to the hospital and university "on the basis of assurances given personally by High Commissioner and the British Secretary of State for Colonies" that medical and civilian traffic would be protected by British forces.

A history published by Hadassah, the American organisation that ran the hospital, fills in the pressure of those months. On 2 March the hospital's telephone exchange received a warning in an Arab voice that the building would be blown up within 90 minutes. It did not happen, but Hadassah's leaders in the United States protested to the State Department, the British embassy, the United Nations and the Red Cross. The same history quotes Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni, the Arab commander, as saying he had given orders "to occupy or even demolish them", meaning the hospital and university, because attacks on Arab homes were being launched from them. Jewish officials, for their part, were weighing whether the hospital could stay open at all. Yassky was told by a surgeon that he could no longer take responsibility for sending cases up to Scopus, and he answered: "The time has not yet come to evacuate Mount Scopus…There is no security anywhere."

The Red Cross had offered to place Scopus under its flag if Hadassah and the university agreed to demilitarize the area, according to the same history. Hadassah's leaders refused, because to them the Red Cross banner was, in that history's phrase, the white flag of surrender. On 10 April Yassky wrote that he was "very pessimistic about Scopus" and that 100,000 Jews of Jerusalem depended on Hadassah functioning somewhere. Three days later he was dead.

Two events from the preceding week hang over every account. The Jerusalem Post says Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni, who led the Arab forces in the city, was killed on 8 April in a Palmach raid; it adds that he had threatened to destroy both the hospital and the university if they were not captured. The following day, on its dating, came the attack on the village of Deir Yassin by the Irgun and Lehi, which the paper says killed what many estimate to be around 100 Arabs. The Hadassah history puts Deir Yassin on 8 April and speaks of as many as 250 Arabs slain.

The Center for Israel Education says the convoy attack is seen as Arab retaliation for Deir Yassin, and the Jerusalem Post says it is thought the earlier events inspired a retaliation. The Hadassah history says otherwise: that the ambush "was not retaliation for the Deir Yassin attack since the Arabs had planned the ambush beforehand," although Deir Yassin was cited to justify it. A Jewish bus guard who survived, Nathan Sandowsky, told of hearing attackers shout "Minshan Deir Yassin," meaning "for Deir Yassin."

The Hadassah history also argues that the ground suited an ambush. Between Nashashibi Bend and Antonius House, a stretch of a few hundred yards, stone walls ran along both sides of a narrow road that climbed slowly and then turned sharply. Vehicles caught there would, it says, be "tin ducks in a shooting gallery." A small unit of Highland Light Infantry sat in Antonius House, but, the history says, it would not fire without orders. On 11 April, it adds, the British commander in Jerusalem assured questioners that the road was safe.

At about 8 a.m. people gathered at the Hasolel Street clinic, where a Hebrew University bus and a Hadassah bus, both lightly armoured, were waiting. Two armoured ambulances stood nearby; Yassky and his wife Fanny rode in one of them, a converted truck painted white with a large Star of David the day before. According to the Hadassah history the exact number of people travelling was never known because no lists were kept, but it was well over 100.

Accounts of the column's make-up differ slightly. Dov Joseph lists two ambulances, three armoured buses, three trucks of food and hospital supplies and two small escort cars. The Center for Israel Education and the Jerusalem Post also count three buses; the Hadassah history and Hadassah's own anniversary story speak of two. Most give the column as ten vehicles. Joseph says it set out at 9:30 a.m. after the British police officer responsible had given the usual assurance that the road was clear. The Hadassah history says that officer, Inspector Robert Webb, normally drove or waited on the route before a convoy and on this day did not take up his post, and that the Haganah could not reach him afterwards.

In the lead escort vehicle Zizi Rahav noticed there was no traffic and that a grocer's shop was shuttered. By his watch it was 9:45 when a mine was detonated electrically in front of his truck and left a ditch about four feet deep. The front wheels dropped in. Behind him the last vehicles tried to turn back. Rahav later recalled that at Nashashibi Bend two British armoured cars blocked the way out, and that he ordered a few bursts fired at them to make them move. He did not know, the Hadassah history says, that one of the cars carried Lieutenant-General G.H.A. MacMillan, the senior British commander in Palestine.

Five vehicles got away, according to the Jerusalem Post. The Hadassah history says the six-ton truck of driver Benjamin Adin reached the Mandelbaum Gate with no foot brakes and flat tyres, and that the larger ambulance's wounded driver turned around and was the first to return. What remained was an ambulance, two Haganah escort vehicles and the two buses. The buses, fifty yards or so behind the head of the column, were, in the Hadassah history's words, "the most open to attack from both sides of the road."

Joseph describes grenades and Molotov cocktails as well as rifle and machine-gun fire. Fire continued through the morning. The Arab attackers were reinforced at noon, he writes, and by three o'clock the two buses had been set alight and most of those still inside "were burned alive."

Two men, one from each bus, are said to have lived. Shalom Nissan, a student, jumped when grenades began landing around his bus and ran to Mount Scopus, giving the first account of the ambush. Sandowsky, a guard, described from the second bus how the drivers had been hit or frozen and how the passengers shouted for help to British convoys that passed without stopping. When the fire began he dived out with a scalpel, the only weapon he had, and ran to an escort car where he found everyone dead or wounded. It was then, by his account, about 2:30 p.m. He later took a machine gun there and kept the attackers back until the British collected the men inside.

In the ambulance that sheltered behind the two Haganah vehicles, Yassky sat beside the driver with a revolver, looking out through a small window. A colleague, Dr. Yehuda Bromberg, recalled that each time he opened it a hail of shots followed. At about 2 p.m., Bromberg reported, Yassky told those inside that everyone in the burning buses had been killed. At about 2:30 a bullet wounded him in the liver. He lost consciousness and died within minutes, the history says, with no first-aid kit in the vehicle. His wife, seeing someone weep, asked why, since they would soon follow him. The ambulance driver, Zecharya Leitan, got out and was shot a few yards away.

A pediatrician in the ambulance, Dr. Yehuda Mattot, crawled to Antonius House and was taken in by the British soldiers, who he said were apologetic and told him they had asked for reinforcements and received none. Elsewhere on the road, Haganah attempts to reach the column failed. Joseph writes that two Haganah cars sent down were ambushed and two from Mount Scopus were mined. Among the dead was an armorer, Baruch Nussbaum, who had crawled towards Antonius House at 12:15 to ask for help, and whose body was found afterwards in a wadi.

The question of British conduct is the most contested part of the story. The Jerusalem Post says the reasons for the delay "are still debated." The Haganah and Hadassah versions are blunt. Joseph says the attack happened less than 200 yards from the British military post responsible for the road, that the soldiers watched and did nothing, and that British military cars passing at 1 p.m. and 2 p.m. were hailed by Yassky and did not stop. When the Jewish Agency liaison officer asked British headquarters to let the Haganah go to the scene, Joseph says, he was told the army had the situation in hand and that Haganah intervention would worsen the fighting. Dr. Judah Magnes, the university's president, telephoned MacMillan for help at 1:45 p.m. and was told a large battle had developed.

MacMillan's own explanation, quoted in the Hadassah history from his reply to Magnes two days later, was that he had passed through at 9:45 under the fire of an automatic weapon from a Jewish armoured car, and "assumed that the situation was clearing up and my inference at the time was that it would have cleared up much quicker, had the Jewish armored car stopped firing." He wrote that on returning at 4:30 p.m. he found Brigadier Jones had persuaded the Arabs to stop firing, but only after forcing his men to fire heavily and kill fifteen. The Hadassah history says Jones was given permission to use bazookas at about 4 p.m., that some mortars were fired, and that half-tracks went in under a smokescreen to pick up survivors. It says volunteers monitoring British radio traffic heard a forward observer say the buses were burning and ask permission to intervene, and headquarters reply that reinforcements were on the way.

One British officer is named in the accounts as having tried to help. Major Jack Churchill of the Highland Light Infantry drove an armoured car to the buses on his own initiative, the Hadassah history says, and was about to attach a towline when his driver was killed by a bullet. Churchill banged on a bus and told those inside to risk getting out with him; he later reported that they refused. The Jerusalem Post also names Churchill among those who eventually intervened.

The Jerusalem Post goes further than other accounts: according to documents held by Hadassah, it says, British mandatory personnel "cooperated and participated" in the attack, and no British collaborators were ever investigated. It adds that the two survivors of the buses testified that British forces nearby refused to help, and that many of the facts remain debated. The Israel Ministry of Defense memorial page for one of the dead guards says British forces on the spot did not intervene, despite appeals, until early evening, when they rescued survivors. The Hadassah history itself suggests only an understanding that the Arabs "would not be disturbed in their mission so long as they did not shoot at British soldiers", and presents this as something "subsequent events indicate", not as a documented arrangement.

Arab statements recorded in these sources sit at odds with the Jewish account. Joseph writes that the Arab Higher Committee claimed the attack had been commanded by an Iraqi officer and praised it as a heroic exploit, adding that it censured the British for their late intervention: "Had it not been for Army interference, not a single Jewish passenger would have remained alive." The Jerusalem Post says the Arabs claimed they had attacked a military formation and that, since the civilians were also fighting, they could not tell soldiers from civilians. The same paper says the attack drew condemnation as an assault on a humanitarian convoy.

Nobody settled the toll. Dov Joseph wrote of 77 dead and 28 saved, 8 of them unhurt. Hadassah's anniversary account counts 78, including Yassky and 77 other hospital personnel, students and soldiers. The Jerusalem Post and the Center for Israel Education say 79; the paper adds that 23 women and one British soldier were among them. The marble memorial near Nashashibi Bend, according to the Hadassah history, lists 76 names and a seventy-seventh entry reading "Unknown", before the count was raised to 78.

Bodies were burned beyond recognition. The Jerusalem Post says only 31 victims could be identified and buried individually, with the rest in a mass grave in Sanhedria Cemetery and 22 still thought to be missing. The Hadassah history gives the same arithmetic from another angle: three days after the attack Hadassah gave the Red Cross a list of forty-seven people "still unaccounted for", and in the mid-1970s an inquiry commission reportedly found that only 25 bodies lay in Sanhedria. Yehoshua Levanon, whose father Zvi was among the dead, later found an Arab who claimed to have taken part in the ambush and who said the remains of 22 were in an Arab cemetery outside the Old City wall; the history says officials doubted this. In late 1996, it adds, Israel's Defense Ministry announced a genetic database to help identify the Sanhedria remains.

The dead came from across Jerusalem's professional life. Joseph lists Yassky, Dr. Leonid Doljansky, Dr. Moshe Ben-David, the physicist Dr. Guenther Wolfsohn and Professor Enzo Bonaventura, head of the university's psychology department. A Hebrew blog by a volunteer researcher at the Yad Ben-Zvi photograph archive says the university lost six lecturers and researchers and the hospital lost its director and another doctor. Joseph calls Yassky, Doljansky and Ben-David founders of the university's new medical faculty, and the blog says the 1952 memorial lecture, held on the anniversary of the medical school's opening, was dedicated to those three. A funeral for the university's dead was held in Jerusalem the next day. The blog author notes (my translation) that the public came to call it the Hadassah convoy even though one of the buses carried university staff with no tie to Hadassah. Ordinary members of the Haganah died too; the Ministry of Defense page records Mordechai Mansour, born in Jerusalem in 1910 to a family from Yemen, a university guard who escorted the convoy, as buried at Sanhedria and survived by his wife and four children.
content.h2: The end of Scopus as a hospital
content.p: Before the dead were all counted the hospital had in effect lost its battle for the hill. The Hadassah history says Dr. Eli Davis, the deputy medical director, negotiated with Major Churchill, who agreed to lead a jeep up to Scopus through Sheikh Jarrah; nothing happened on the way. Davis then arranged a large evacuation, with four convoys bringing down 200 patients, 100 student nurses and 300 staff, together with 600 tons of equipment and supplies, without a shot fired. A 50-bed hospital was kept on the hill and some 150 people stayed, plus 150 men in university buildings. On 6 May the administrator, Haim Halevy, reported: "The hospital no longer exists for all practical purposes."

The Haganah, then under a young Palmach officer named Yitzhak Rabin, occupied Nashashibi House on 25 April, the Hadassah history says, but was shelled out by the British the next day. Judah Magnes, according to the same history, was shattered by British nonchalance over the convoy and wrote to MacMillan: "This happened not out in the desert but in plain sight of Jerusalem." He left for the United States and died in October 1948.

The Jerusalem Post says the hospital later became a demilitarised enclave in Jordanian-controlled East Jerusalem and was not reopened until after the Six Day War. Meanwhile the doctors who had gone down set up in the city, in what became Hadassah Ein Kerem.

Hadassah's Mount Scopus hospital still marks the attack. At a ceremony described by the organisation 74 years after the attack, wreaths were laid in the memorial garden, where a plaque lists the names of the dead. Shooky Levanon, who was two when his father Zvi, a Hadassah technician, was killed, spoke; a passage from his book had his father saying "Help has to come," and the organisation adds that it never did. Jerusalem's deputy mayor, Elisha Peleg, said the convoy taught Israel it could not rely on others for its defence, and of the dead: "They have not died in vain."

The record leaves several things open. The accounts do not agree on whether the buses numbered two or three, on whether the toll was 77, 78 or 79, on how long the attack lasted, or on whether the date was 13 or 14 April. They disagree over whether the attack was retaliation for Deir Yassin or planned beforehand. The extent of British responsibility, from negligence to what Hadassah's documents and the Jerusalem Post call complicity, has never been tested in a court. According to the Jerusalem Post, no one was ever prosecuted.
